title: Ofcom's Online Safety Act: Slow Progress and Missing Teeth?
label: 15 Sep 2026 · Online Safety Act implementation
summary: Ofcom's online safety team gave evidence to the Communications and Digital Committee about how the Online Safety Act is being implemented. They explained that most duties are now in force but the full regime won't be operational until mid-2027. They admitted progress has been slower and less visible than hoped, with frustrations about enforcement, limited powers to force companies to use proactive technology, and a safe harbour that lets companies off the hook if they follow the codes. They called for targeted reforms to strengthen their ability to hold platforms to account.

speakers.label: Mark Bunting
speakers.name: Mark Bunting
speakers.role: Director, Online Safety Strategy Delivery, Ofcom

chapters.title: Where the Act stands
chapters.takeaway: Most online safety duties are now in force, but the final piece for the biggest platforms won't be finished until mid-2027.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome. This is our second evidence session on the Online Safety Act. Ofcom is the UK's online safety regulator, so we're pleased to have you here. Could you introduce yourselves?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: I'm Oliver Griffiths, group director for online safety at Ofcom.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: I'm Suzanne Cater, director of enforcement at Ofcom, with primary responsibility for enforcing the Online Safety Act.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: I'm Mark Bunting, director of strategy delivery in Ofcom's online safety group, responsible for our overall strategic direction.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Act passed in 2023. Which parts are now in effect and what's still to come?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: There are three main planks: duties on illegal harms, duties to protect children from certain legal material, and extra duties for categorised services — those are the biggest platforms. We prioritised getting the first two into force quickly. Those took about 18 months from passage. The children's codes came into force in early 2025.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: The third plank was delayed by a legal challenge from Wikimedia about how we categorise services. That finished last summer. We published the list of categorised services and consulted on their duties. That consultation is about to wrap up.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: The Act has also been amended, for example by the Crime and Policing Act, which added new priority offences like cyber stalking and serious health harm. We'll consult later this year on a 48-hour takedown duty for non-consensual intimate images.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We expect the categorised services duties to be fully in force by around mid-2027. But the Government's new plans for a social media ban for under-16s and possible AI regulation are changing things, and we're in talks about what that means for our work and resources.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So the full regime won't be operational until mid-2027?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: Yes, that's our current programme, but it depends on ongoing discussions with Government about sequencing.

chapters.title: Extra work and lessons learned
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom was already fully stretched, and the new social media ban means more money and staff are needed to avoid delays.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What impact will the under-16 social media ban have on your timetable?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We were fully loaded before the ban was announced. We've moved staff onto it, but without extra funding something has to give. The Government committed in June to extra funding, and we submitted a detailed business plan in July. We're in talks about both funding and sequencing. We'll set out a revised roadmap by the end of the year. It's doable if it's resourced and sequenced right.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What lessons have you learned from the first two phases?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: One is about consultation. We published our first proposals very quickly after the Act passed, before we'd had much time to engage with industry or civil society. It was the right call to move fast, but we've learned to engage better. For example, our work on women and girls was much more collaborative with the women's sector and services.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: The second is the safe harbour in the Act. That's where companies are deemed compliant if they follow our codes of practice. It gives clarity, but it can also limit us: if a company ticks all the boxes in the code, we can't easily force them to do more about risks they've identified.

chapters.title: Risk assessments and children's safety
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom hasn't given the Children's Commissioner risk assessments because companies must consent, but it's willing to ask them if a formal request is made.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Children's Commissioner told us she asked to see the risk assessments that online services must produce, and Ofcom wouldn't provide them. Can you explain?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We work closely with the Commissioner, who runs a children's panel for us. On this point, we haven't received a formal request. Under Section 393 of the Act, we need the company's consent before sharing with a third party. If she makes a formal request, we'll ask the companies if they're happy to share. That's the process we must follow.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If she does make a formal request, you'll be prepared to let her see them?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We'll go to the companies and check they're happy, as the Act requires. Absolutely, we'll follow that process.

turns.speaker: Baroness Caine of Kentish Town
turns.text: Was there an informal approach?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: There have been discussions with the teams for months.

chapters.title: Has the Act made people safer?
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom says there's been real progress on age checks for porn and some big platforms, but overall the effect so far is underwhelming and culture change takes time.

turns.speaker: Lord Storey
turns.text: Has the Online Safety Act made children and adults in the UK safer online?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: That's the fundamental question. We've seen big changes. Our survey of 125 companies found 76% had completed a risk assessment, 44% had made changes, and 59% felt they'd fully or substantively implemented the requirements. There are 100,000 services in scope.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: The most visible change is age assurance — that means checking someone's age before they can access certain content. Since July last year, big services like Reddit, X and Discord have put age gates in place. In the pornography sector, all top-10 services now have age gates, and three-quarters of the top 100 either have them or have blocked UK access. We've seen a 23-fold increase in age checks across 32 companies.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Less visibly, some services have chosen to block UK access entirely when we contact them about their obligations. That happened with a prominent suicide forum and some file-sharing sites with child sexual abuse material.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: But we're less content with some big services most used by children. We secured commitments from X on hate and terror takedown times, and from Meta and Snap on grooming. Overall, our tracking shows we're underwhelmed by the effect so far. This is a one-way ratchet that will build up over time.

turns.speaker: Lord Storey
turns.text: The Children's Commissioner said the Act has made 'absolutely no difference'. How do you respond?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We share the frustration. We're trying to change corporate cultures that have built up over decades. The Act drives change through risk assessments rather than taking down content, to change incentives for leaders. That takes time, especially across so many sectors. I came into this job to make life better, especially for children, but we're still early in the journey.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We've seen steps along the road, but there's a long way to go. For example, some big firms have committed to making it harder for strangers to approach children, but we're not sure they have good enough ways of identifying who the children are. You can change one system but not the whole system.

turns.speaker: Lord Storey
turns.text: Should society allow tech companies to operate if they can't guarantee children's safety?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: The Act says there's no freedom to operate if you can't keep people safe. The duties are on the companies. Society doesn't accept the current situation.

turns.speaker: Lord Storey
turns.text: Will there come a time when you say, 'We'll take you down, you can't operate in the UK'?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: If we suspect a breach, we can launch an enforcement case. If they don't comply, we can apply to a court for a business disruption measure, which stops their access to the UK. That's not taking down the site globally — our reach only goes as far as the UK — but it's a powerful tool.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do you think children's real-life experience online has improved?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: There's good anecdotal evidence things are moving in the right direction. We have a big monitoring and evaluation programme. But AI is supercharging harms like creating child sexual abuse material, so it's a mixed picture.

chapters.title: Gaming and safe harbour
chapters.takeaway: Gaming is a focus but not top priority; the safe harbour lets companies off the hook if they follow codes, and Ofcom wants a duty to mitigate all risks.

turns.speaker: Baroness Caine of Kentish Town
turns.text: What progress in gaming?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Some gaming services like Xbox and Steam have introduced age gates. It's important but not front and centre — we've prioritised social media and child protection.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We focus on interactions between users. On Roblox, we've seen evidence of people who wish children harm. Our recommended controls on age verification and preventing adults approaching unknown children have been effective. But broader issues like violence and screen time aren't captured by the Act. Our engagement is narrow but focused where we can make a difference.

turns.speaker: Viscount Colville of Culross
turns.text: You've said you want targeted reforms, including reviewing the safe harbour. Would you like to see it taken out?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: It's complicated. The Act created two parallel frameworks: a risk-based duty and the codes with safe harbour. If companies do everything in our codes, they're deemed compliant even if risks remain. That's a tension. We can't enforce against them if they've ticked the boxes.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: The reason I can't give a straight answer is that the safe harbour gives legal certainty, which also helps us enforce. If we're not clear what companies must do, it's hard to win investigations. We'd be stronger with a duty to mitigate all risks, even beyond codes, but that would be harder to enforce and not a quick route to fines.

turns.speaker: Viscount Colville of Culross
turns.text: Why difficult to enforce against companies that haven't mitigated?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: Enforcement is easiest with a clear requirement, like age verification. A broad duty to do everything reasonable opens lengthy legal debates. That's the tension.

turns.speaker: Viscount Colville of Culross
turns.text: Would a duty of care help — where providers must ensure new products don't harm users?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: The word 'proportionate' isn't the problem; it's the safe harbour and codes. Schedule 4 says codes must contain clear and detailed steps, putting the onus on us to specify actions. We think that's an area Government might look at.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: The codes must be accessible to a huge range of services. We have to balance clear rules with flexibility. A duty of care is an alternative, but you'd still need to define parameters carefully, especially for small services. The largest services often have sophisticated measures but not enough to address harm, and they argue they're within safe harbour, so we can't enforce further.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What about safety by design, expecting platforms to be safe by design?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: The Act is all about safety by design — we don't regulate content, we focus on how services are designed and governed. But the safe harbour limits it. Safety by design should put the onus on companies to identify what they need to do, not on us to spell it out.

chapters.title: Enforcement and emerging harms
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom says it's using its powers, but legal challenges and slow processes make it hard; it wants to do more but faces practical limits.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fleet
turns.text: You said many big companies are 'not yet doing enough'. The Molly Rose Foundation says teenagers' exposure to suicide, self-harm and eating disorder content has barely changed. What's stopping you going faster?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: On proactive monitoring, companies can either wait for reports or use tools to detect harmful content before users see it. Some firms say they use automated tools, but we haven't seen data to assess effectiveness. We're consulting on requiring them more widely.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: The Act set high thresholds for requiring these tools due to privacy and free expression concerns. We're gathering evidence and will say more this autumn. It's not clear the Act forces companies to use them.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fleet
turns.text: That seems like a fundamental flaw.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: It's not had much discussion. We must think carefully because scanning all material is intrusive. But the case is strong and we're working on proposals.

turns.speaker: Baroness Elliott of Whitburn Bay
turns.text: Stakeholders say Ofcom is slow, reactive, not flexible. Why so sluggish?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: When Grok on X emerged over Christmas, we launched an investigation within two weeks. We have 140 priority offences. We're in constant dialogue with Government and law enforcement. We can move quickly when needed — faster than international peers.

turns.speaker: Baroness Elliott of Whitburn Bay
turns.text: Sir Jeremy Wright said the Act doesn't require you to know something will work before trying it. Are you too cautious?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We've published our risk appetites — on legal, we have an open risk appetite. But we operate in a highly litigious environment. Meta is running judicial reviews against us on fees, services are challenging our data collection, and four are appealing categorisation. If we run unnecessary risks, we'll get clobbered legally. We're learning as we go.

turns.speaker: Baroness Elliott of Whitburn Bay
turns.text: Why do stakeholders perceive you as slow?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: The Act is extraordinarily broad — over 100,000 services. We must focus to drive systemic change. Choosing means other areas get less focus. That's inevitable.

turns.speaker: Lord Kirkhope of Harrogate
turns.text: The perception is you don't use your teeth. Is it legal constraints or reluctance?

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: I agree we must use our teeth. There's a perception problem. Enforcement is critical, especially for a sector never regulated before. We need to make leaders believe we'll act and impose meaningful penalties.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: We are using our teeth. We've opened six enforcement programmes, 40 formal investigations covering 100 services. We imposed £7 million in penalties. We're shifting to bigger cases like X, Telegram, TikTok. We're starting to use senior management liability powers.

turns.speaker: Lord Kirkhope of Harrogate
turns.text: In the suicide forum case, you said you ran out of legal routes. Are your tools inadequate?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We've been the most active international regulator. But these things take time — EU, Australia, US all take 2-3 years. We want to be quicker, but we're at that stage. Business disruption measures have issues.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: Many services are small and overseas with no UK assets, making enforcement hard. Some haven't paid penalties. We're pursuing judgment debts, but overseas enforcement is limited. Business disruption requires ongoing non-compliance; if a service withdraws from the UK, we can't apply. If they comply but don't pay fines, we can't use it. That would be helpful.

chapters.title: VPNs, fines and the Meta settlement
chapters.takeaway: VPNs are a political decision; Ofcom doesn't keep fines; the US Meta settlement is instructive but doesn't mean Ofcom will seek huge sums.

turns.speaker: Viscount Colville of Culross
turns.text: On the suicide forum, should the Act be amended to force companies to deal with VPNs?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: That's a political decision outside our remit. VPN use went up after age gates, but not massively. Australia said 8% of non-compliant children used VPNs. It could grow. Government is considering recommendations. We'll do what we're told.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How much of the £7 million in fines has been collected?

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: I don't have a figure, but I know we had another payment this week. The majority hasn't been paid. We'll follow up.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Early fines were on smaller porn sites. As we move to bigger sites with UK assets, this will reduce.

turns.speaker: Baroness Caine of Kentish Town
turns.text: Do you have enough resources? Could fines help?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Culture change is key. International regulation and US litigation will change incentives. CFOs provisioning for damages focuses minds. Data protection is a good analogy. Fines must accompany that. We don't keep fines — they go to the Treasury. We're funded by companies, not the public purse.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: On VPNs, the Minister said providers must account for VPN use. Do you agree?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: I don't think the Act requires preventing VPN use. We've acted against firms encouraging VPNs. But a ban on VPN access is a bigger debate.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: The Meta settlement in the US was eye-catching — $18 billion. Does that change your approach to fines?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: It changes the game by bringing safety to executives' attention. Our penalties are capped at 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue. We have those numbers from the fees regime. We won't be swayed by $18 billion. And we don't keep fines — they go to the Treasury.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: The settlement was about system design. Is that instructive?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: Much of it aligns with our framework. But it went further on features like screen time and addictive effects, which the Act didn't cover.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: Should it?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: That's for Government and Parliament.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: The Government has made commitments on curfews and time limits. The Meta settlement is one company, for 5-10 years, not in perpetuity. I wouldn't be too tough on the Act.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: Could you apply the settlement's elements across all platforms?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Our powers are bound by the Act. We called out big companies for not policing minimum age. We don't have power to enforce that, but we encourage them to go further. If they commit in one jurisdiction, we'd like them to commit here.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: Would going after recklessness, like health and safety law, be better?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We're early days. There are dangers in throwing babies out with bathwater. Targeted interventions could improve it. The UK doesn't have the same civic litigation culture. The principle of putting the duty on companies is good. We're still early.

chapters.title: What single change would help most
chapters.takeaway: Each witness named one reform: a duty to mitigate all risks, better business disruption measures, and easier use of proactive technology.

turns.speaker: Lord Tarassenko
turns.text: What single change to the Act would make the greatest difference?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: A duty to address all identified risks, linked to duty of care. It needs careful thought, but it would give us more scope to engage big firms on the totality of their risk management.

turns.speaker: Lord Tarassenko
turns.text: Have you looked at Australia's digital duty of care?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We'd need to think carefully about how it fits with the existing framework. It's not a quick fix.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: I'd reform business disruption measures. They're our strongest enforcement tool but have practical challenges. Amendments to make them work better would make a big difference.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: I'd make it easier to force companies to use proactive technology to control the content served to users. That's a narrow, specific change that would help a lot.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. We've had useful discussions. We'll write to you for more detail on those points.
